prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, which brought the measurement of time to the 10^-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: I opened with circuit QED first, but on reflection I move the optical lattice clock to the top of my own list. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal is a clean idea, and it was turned into working instruments by Katori and Ye. These are clocks in which the atoms' motion no longer limits the measurement, with accuracy near 10^-18 and many-body effects now visible in the systematics. That is a clear new regime of measurement that makes basic quantum physics visible and controllable, which is the kind of result I value most. It has been reproduced and compared across JILA, RIKEN, SYRTE, PTB and NIST, with fibre and optical comparisons between institutes. Its consequences (tests of constancy of constants, relativistic redshift over millimetres, preparation for a redefinition of the second) are consequences of the discovery, not the reason for it. Three colleagues placed it first, and its maturity and attribution (a natural two-person set) are the most settled on the shortlist.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that much of the enabling physics was already rewarded: Hall and Haensch for the frequency comb in 2005 and Wineland and Haroche for quantum control of single particles in 2012. A committee could see lattice clocks as an excellent, long, incremental refinement of precision spectroscopy and not a discrete discovery. The two-name set also leaves out theory and parallel-development credit (Lemonde, Derevianko and the ion-clock community), which I cannot fully judge from the supplied material. If the committee wants a conceptual opening of a new field rather than a record of precision, magic-angle graphene or circuit QED has the stronger claim.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock first as a decisive step in measurement precision with long coherence times and small systematic shifts, and a two-person prize is clean, while he places circuit QED fifth because of overlap with the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I agree with the attribution and I am persuaded by the overlap argument about circuit QED. The 2025 prize was about macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, and circuit QED is a distinct discovery, but awarding two consecutive prizes in superconducting circuits would look less convincing to me, and I am an interested party. I would qualify his point on the frequency comb: the comb overlap is real, but the lattice clock's own physics (the magic wavelength, which removes the lattice light shift, and the Fermi-gas many-body shifts) is not in the comb prize, so I do not think it is incremental.

responses.point: Lindroth places the lattice clock first because it tests fundamental physics and rests on a clean, easily explained idea, but she admits she recalls the facts from memory and flags credit for theory contributions that are not in the list.
responses.response: I support her reading of the physics. Where I would push back on a point implicit in her second place for B017 is that the atom-simulation case needs a decisive new result, and I do not think quantum simulation has yet delivered one that quantum-gas microscopy alone did not already demonstrate. On the theory credit for clocks (Derevianko and others), I think the committee can accept that the prize goes to the proposal and its realisation, but this deserves a check of the record before the final ballot.

responses.point: Olsson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first because the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states opened a tunable platform, with the Bistritzer-MacDonald theory showing where to look, and she sees timing as reasonable even though the pairing mechanism is debated.
responses.response: I find the theory-plus-experiment story compelling, and it is my own third choice. My concern is stability of the interpretation: sample-to-sample variation and twist-angle disorder complicate the reproducibility story, and the superconducting mechanism is unsettled. I would not call it premature, but I would hold the prize until the pairing question is clearer, unless the committee chooses to reward only the discovery of the correlated phases and the flat-band prediction. The omission of Cao and Fatemi is a real attribution cost that the other candidates do not carry to the same degree.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks the topological insulator set first as a clear case of a bold theoretical prediction confirmed by experiment, and stresses fifteen years of independent confirmation, while noting the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap.
responses.response: I rank it second and agree on the physics. Where I disagree is on its readiness as a prize configuration: with Zhang deceased and the HgTe proposal outside the credited names, the three-person set seems a compromise for an experiment (Molenkamp) that followed a proposal from outside it. The 2016 prize also covered topological phases, so I would like to see how Kane, Mele and Molenkamp are distinguished from it before I call this the best choice.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as a discrete discovery or as a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes.
How much credit for the lattice-clock concept belongs to theory and to other lattice-clock groups outside Katori and Ye.
Whether the twisted bilayer graphene superconductivity question will be resolved enough to make the moire prize safe.
Whether the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize makes circuit QED too soon, or whether it should be treated as a separate achievement.
statement.conflict_note: I direct WACQT and work in superconducting circuits, and I know the circuit QED groups (Wallraff, Schoelkopf, Blais) and the 2025 laureates, who were guest researchers at Chalmers. I should recuse myself or at least discount my own view on B004. I have no specific connection to the optical lattice clock, graphene, topological insulator or other shortlisted candidates apparent from my profile.
